newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Troubled Yugoslavian banks face liquidation.
newsitem.headline: Troubled Yugoslavian banks face liquidation.

text.p: Insolvent Yugoslav banks may face a wave of liquidations if they fail to meet new criteria set by the central bank, analysts said on Tuesday.

Reacting to the sudden dinar plunge over the New Year holidays, the National Bank of Yugoslavia (NBY) said late last week it was taking decisive measures to save the dinar and restore financial discipline.

NBY will halt further growth in the money supply, prevent imbalances on the banks' giro-accounts, halt insolvent banks from further lending activity and take other measures to establish financial discipline, the statement said.
"Those measures have already yielded results. We only want to prevent further deteriorating of financial discipline," a senior NBY official, who asked not to be named, told Reuters.
A rigorous action by NBY was needed to prevent growth in M1 money supply, inflation and changes in the dinar rate, it said.
"Persistently insolvent banks will have their licences revoked," the source added.
But the destiny of those banks is in the hands of local courts, which decide whether a bank will be a candidate for rehabilitation, acquired by a larger bank or liquidated.
The NBY source insisted there was no point in forcing big, equally troubled banks into acquiring smaller insolvent ones.
"If a big troubled bank acquires a smaller insolvent one, you only produce an insolvent giant," Stojan Stamenkovic of the Institute of Economic Sciences said.
Stamenkovic said it was uncertain how far NBY can go with this purge of the banking system and whether the process will be in conflict with the state interests.
"This is too much for this shrunken market. Only three to four banks are truly servicing companies," one banker said.
Zoran Pavlovic, spokesman for the largest commercial bank Beobanka, said the banking system was oversized, irrational and inefficient. He expected radical changes in months to come.
"But first of all, we expect monetary authorities to tighten regulations for issuing bank licences," Pavlovic said.
He said big banks will only suffer damage if they are forced into acquisitions. "Who is going to take over responsibility for hard currency savings?" he said.
Yugoslav banks are burdened with more than $4 billion in so-called hard currency savings, frozen in the early 1990s.
The state has delayed a solution to the problem, crucial to revive savings in the country where citizens are estimated to hide at least three billion German marks in their mattresses.

"The state will have to find a consistent solution. No miracles should be expected, but it must take over majority of the debt and pay it back in five to 10 years," head of the Economics Institute Danko Djunic said.
